transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started. As you all know, we're facing a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit from a former employee, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. We have an initial case-management conference next month, and no discovery has been exchanged yet. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs under control. Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need discovery counsel and insurance-coverage counsel to identify any facts that should shape our approach. Let's start with discovery counsel — what do we need to know to build our protective strategy?

transcript.text: Elena, there's a critical fact that should shape our entire defense strategy. My forensic review of the former employee's company laptop has been completed. The findings are significant: exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device, but I found no customer data on it, and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. This report is awaiting final partner review and hasn't yet been added to the case plan. Knowing the scope is limited to three specific files should fundamentally change our approach — we can push back hard against the broad inspection demands in the complaint by demonstrating that the actual exposure is narrow and identifiable, rather than opening up all devices and systems to sweeping discovery. This also helps contain costs because we can propose a targeted discovery protocol rather than a forensic free-for-all.

transcript.text: Elena, before we finalize the defense plan, I need to flag several insurance-coverage constraints that will directly shape our approach. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and the trade-secret defense is covered — but subject to four conditions: first, a $75,000 self-insured retention; second, we must use insurer-approved panel counsel; third, we need written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor; and fourth, we must notify the insurer as part of the approved defense plan. The endorsement is stored in the risk department's file and has not yet been attached to this matter. This is critical right now because Samir has already completed a forensic review — if that vendor was engaged without prior written insurer consent, we may have a coverage issue. We need to get the endorsement into this matter file immediately, confirm whether the forensic vendor was insurer-approved, and notify the insurer as part of the defense plan before any further work is done.

transcript.text:
Thank you both — this is exactly why we hold these planning meetings before I approve anything. Let me synthesize what I'm hearing and identify the key issues we need to resolve.

First, Samir, your forensic findings are significant. If the exposure is limited to three identified trade-secret files with no customer data and no additional copying, that fundamentally supports a push for a narrow protective order and a targeted discovery protocol rather than broad inspection. That aligns directly with our priorities of protecting confidential information and controlling costs.

But Morgan raises a critical concern that we need to address before anything else. Samir, your forensic review is already complete — but Morgan is telling us the insurance endorsement requires prior written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor. If that consent wasn't obtained, we may have a coverage problem. So I need to know from you, Samir: was the forensic vendor engaged with prior written insurer consent, and was it an insurer-approved panel vendor? And Morgan, I need the endorsement pulled into this matter file immediately so we can verify all four conditions you've identified.

Here's what I'm considering for the defense plan: we push for a narrow protective order and targeted discovery scope limited to the three identified files, we do not produce customer data since none was found on the device, we use insurer-approved panel counsel, we account for the $75,000 self-insured retention, we require insurer consent for any forensic vendor going forward, and we notify the insurer as part of the approved plan. But I cannot approve this plan until we resolve whether the forensic work already done jeopardizes our coverage. Can both of you confirm the status on the vendor consent question?

transcript.text: Elena, that's a fair and important question, and I want to be straightforward with you. Based on what I know, I conducted the forensic review of the former employee's company laptop, but I do not have information confirming whether the vendor was engaged with prior written insurer consent or whether it was an insurer-approved panel vendor. That's simply not something that was within the scope of what I was given or asked to verify when the forensic work was initiated. So I cannot confirm either way on the vendor consent question right now. What I can tell you is what I've already shared: the forensic findings themselves are solid — three identified trade-secret files copied, no customer data, no evidence of additional copying — and that report is awaiting final partner review. I agree with Morgan that we need to pull the endorsement into the matter file immediately and verify whether the vendor engagement met the policy conditions. If it turns out consent wasn't obtained, we'll need to address that with the insurer as part of the defense plan notification. But the forensic findings themselves should still inform our discovery strategy regardless of the coverage question — the scope of exposure is narrow and identifiable, and that supports pushing back against broad inspection demands at the case-management conference.

transcript.text: Thank you, Samir. I appreciate the candor. The fact that you can't confirm whether the vendor was insurer-approved or whether prior written consent was obtained is itself a red flag we need to address immediately. Here's what I recommend from a coverage standpoint: First, I will pull the endorsement from the risk department's file into this matter today so we have the full policy terms in front of us. Second, we need to identify who authorized the forensic vendor engagement and whether any coverage conditions were communicated to them at the time — that may be something Elena can help trace through the matter intake process. Third, I strongly recommend we notify the insurer now, as part of presenting the defense plan, and be transparent about the forensic work already completed. If we approach the insurer proactively rather than waiting for them to discover it later, we're in a much stronger position to argue for coverage despite any technical non-compliance with the consent requirement. Insurers are often willing to retroactively approve vendor work if the findings are sound and the vendor is qualified — but only if we're upfront about it. Fourth, going forward, no forensic vendor should be engaged without written insurer consent, full stop. Elena, I'd also note that the $75,000 self-insured retention means the company will bear the initial defense costs up to that threshold, so cost discipline on the discovery side — which Samir's narrow-scope approach supports — is doubly important here. I can have the endorsement in the matter file and a draft insurer notification prepared by end of day. Can we agree that the defense plan will include insurer notification and a hold on any further forensic vendor engagement until we have written consent?
